{{RunningHeader|top|6384|toparchia}}{{smaller block|What is this That . . . wears upon his baby-brow the round And ''top'' of sovereignty? {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 1. 89.}}}} {{smaller block|He was a Roman, and the ''top'' of honour. {{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', False One, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''top'' of woman! all her sex in abstract! {{right|''B. Jonson'', Devil is an Ass, iv. 1.}}}} 9. ''Naut.'', a sort of platform surrounding the head of the lower mast on all sides. {{smaller|It serves to extend the topmast-shrouds. The tops are named after the respective masts to which they belong, as ''maintop, foretop'', and ''mizzentop''. See cut under ''lubber''.}} {{smaller block|In the morning we descried from the ''top'' eight sail astern of us. {{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 6.}}}} 10. The cover of a carriage. {{smaller|In coaches it is a permanent cover; in barouches and landaus it is a double calash; in gigs, phaëtons, etc., it is a calash.}} 11. That part of a cut gem which is between the girdle or extreme margin and the table or flat face. ''E. H. Knight.''—12. ''pl.'' Buttons washed or plated with gold, silver, tin, etc., on the face or front side only: when the whole is thus treated, they are called ''all-overs''. [Trade-name.]—13. Same as ''top-boot'': especially in the plural: as, a pair of ''tops''. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|To stand in a bar, . . . in a green coat, knee-cords, and ''tops''. {{right|''Dickens'', Pickwick, xiv.}}}} {{smaller block|It was a kind of festive occasion, and the parties were attired accordingly. Mr. Weller's ''tops'' were newly cleaned, and his dress was arranged with peculiar care. {{right|''Dickens'', Pickwick, lv.}}}} 14. The end-piece of a jointed fishing-rod; the tip; also, the topping or mounting at the end of this piece, usually made of bell-metal, agate, carnelian, etc.—15. A method of cheating at dice in vogue about the beginning of the eighteenth century. {{smaller|Both dice seemed to be put into the box, but in reality one was kept at the top of the box between the fingers of the person playing.}}—'''At the top of one's lungs.''' See ''lung''.—'''Bow top.''' See ''bow''2.—'''Captains of tops.''' See ''captain''.—'''From top to toe''', from head to foot; hence, wholly; entirely; throughout. {{smaller block|Be-hold me how that I ame tourne,
For I ame rente ''fro tope to to.'' {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 95.}}}} '''Lop and top.''' See ''lop''2.—'''On top of''', superimposed on.—'''To cry on''' (or '''in''') '''the top of†''', to speak with greater force or importance than; overrule. {{smaller block|It was—as I received it, and others, whose judgements in such matters ''cried in the top of'' mine—an excellent play. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 2. 459.}}}} '''Top and butt''', in ''ship-building'', a method of working long tapering planks, by laying their broad and narrow ends alternately fore-and-aft, lining a piece off every broad end the whole length of the shifting. It is adopted principally for ceiling. Sometimes used attributively: as, "''top and butt'' . . . fashions," ''Thearle'', Naval Arch., § 213.—'''Top and tail†''', everything; beginning and end. {{smaller block|Thou shalt . . . with thyn eres heren wel
''Top and tail'', and every del. {{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 880.}}}} '''Top and topgallant†''', in complete array; in full rig; in full force. {{smaller block|Captains, he cometh hitherward amain,
''Top and top-gallant'', all in brave array. {{right|''Peele'', Battle of Alcazar, iii. 3.}}}} '''Top of the tree''', the highest point or position attainable; the highest rank in the social scale, in a profession, or the like. {{smaller block|My Lady Dedlock has been . . . at the ''top of the'' fashionable ''tree.'' {{right|''Dickens'', Bleak House, ii.}}}} '''Top over tail†''', heels over head; topsyturvy. {{smaller block|Happili to the hinde he hit thanne formest,
& set hire a sad strok so sore in the necke That sche ''top ouer tail'' tombled ouer the hacches. {{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2776.}}}} '''Top-road bridge.''' See ''bridge.''—'''Tops-and-bottoms,''' small rolls of dough baked, cut in halves, and then browned in an oven, used as food for infants. ''Simmonds.'' {{smaller block|'Tis said that her ''tops and bottoms'' were gilt, Like the oats in that Stable-yard Palace built For the horse of Heliogabalus. {{right|''Hood'', Miss Kilmansegg, Her Birth.}}}} '''II.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Being at the top; uppermost; highest; foremost; first; chief; principal. {{smaller block|These twice-six colts had pace so swift, they ran Upon the ''top''-ayles of corn ears, nor bent them any whit. {{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xx. 211.}} The fine Berinthia, one of the ''Top''-Characters, is impudent and Profane. {{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 219.}} The humble ass serves the poorer sort of people, there being only a few of the ''top'' families in the city [of Scio] who use horses. ''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 9. Aniline colours used alone remained in fashion for a short time only, but are now usefully employed as ''top'' colours—namely, brushed in very dilute solution over vegetable colours. ''Workshop Receipts'', 2d ser., p. 236.}} '''2.''' Greatest; extreme. {{smaller block|Setting out at ''top'' speed, he soon overtook him. {{right|''H. Brooke'', Fool of Quality, I. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''3.''' Prime; good; capital: as, ''top'' ale. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]—'''The top notch.''' See ''notch.''—'''Top and bottom tools,''' striking-tools, such as chisels or punches and swages. The bottom tools have generally square tangs to fit into the square opening in the anvil, and the operator holds the work upon the bottom tool, while {{smaller|the top tool is held above the work, and is struck with a sledge by another workman.—'''Top burton.''' See ''burton.''—'''Top cover,''' the upper or front cover of a book. [Eng.]—'''Top edge,''' the head or upper edge of a book. [Eng.]—'''Top rib,''' in ''gun-making.'' See ''rib''1, 2 (''l'').—'''Top side.''' Same as ''top cover.''}} '''top'''1 (top), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''topped,'' ppr. ''topping.'' [< ''top''1, ''n.'' Cf. ''top''2, ''v.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To put a top on; cap; crown. {{smaller block|Her more famous mountaines are the aforesaid Hæmus, [and] Rhodope still ''topt'' with snow. {{right|''Sandys,'' Travailes, p. 33.}}}} '''2.''' In ''dyeing,'' to cover or wash over with a different or richer color: as, to ''top'' indigo with a bright aniline, to give force and brilliancy.—'''3.''' To place and fasten upon the back margin of (a saw-blade) a stiffening piece, or a gage for limiting the depth of a kerf; back (a saw).—'''4.''' To reach the top of. {{smaller block|Wind about till you have ''topp'd'' the hill. {{right|''Sir J. Denham,'' Prudence.}}}} '''5.''' To rise above or beyond; surmount. {{smaller block|The moon . . . like an enemy broke upon me, ''topping'' the eastward ridge of rock. {{right|''R. D. Blackmore,'' Lorna Doone, xxxvii.}} The sun was just ''topping'' the maples. {{right|''The Century,'' XXVI. 376.}}}} '''6.''' To pass over; leap; clear. {{smaller block|Many a green dog would endeavour to take a meuse instead of ''topping'' the brambles, thereby possibly splitting a claw. {{right|''The Field,'' March 19, 1887. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}} '''7.''' To surpass; outdo. {{smaller block|If this letter speed, And my invention thrive, Edmund the base Shall ''top'' the legitimate. {{right|''Shak.,'' Lear, i. 2. 21.}}}} 8. To take off the top of. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') To remove the top or end from (a plant); especially, to crop, as a tree or plant, by cutting off the growing top, or before ripening (as, in the case of tobacco, to increase the size of the remaining leaves, or, with maize, to hasten the ripening, etc.).}} {{smaller block|What tree if it be not ''topped'' beareth any fruite? {{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 127.}}}} {{smaller block|Periander, being consulted with how to preserve a tyranny newly usurped, . . . went into his garden and ''topped'' all the highest flowers. {{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii.}}}} {{smaller block|(''b'') To snuff (a candle): said also of burning off the long end of a new wick. ''Halliwell; De Vere.'' [Prov. Eng. and U. S.]}} {{smaller block|''Top'' the candle, sirrah; methinks the light burns blue. {{right|''Middleton'', Your Five Gallants, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|(''c'') See the quotation.}} {{smaller block|Harder tempers of steel, containing 0.7 per cent. of carbon and upwards, settle down after teeming, leaving a hollow or funnel-shaped tube or pipe at the top of the ingot, which requires to be broken off, or the ingot ''topped'', as it is called, before working the same. {{right|''W. H. Greenwood'', Steel and Iron, p. 424.}}}} 9. ''Naut.'', to raise one end, as of a yard or boom, higher than the other.—10. To hang. ''Tuft's Glossary of Thieves' Jargon'' (1798). [Thieves' slang.] {{smaller block|Thirty-six were cast for death, and only one was ''topped''. {{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, III. 387.}}}} 11. To tup; cover. ''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2. 136.—'''Topping the dice.''' {{smaller|See ''top''1, ''n.'', 15.}}—'''To top off.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To complete by putting on the top or uppermost part of: as, to ''top off'' a stack of hay; hence, to finish; put the finishing touch to.}} {{smaller block|A heavy sleep evolved out of sauerkraut, sausages, and cider, lightly ''topped off'' with a mountain of crisp waffles. {{right|''The Century'', XLI. 47.}}}} {{smaller|(''b''†) To take or toss off; drink off.}} {{smaller block|Its no heinous offence (beleeve me) for a young man to hunt harlots, to ''toppe of'' a canne roundly; its no great fault to breake open dores. {{right|''Terence in English'' (1614). (''Nares.'')}}}} {{smaller|'''To top one's part''', to do one's part with zeal and success; outdo one's self.}} {{smaller block|Well, Jenny, you ''topp'd your part'', indeed. {{right|''Steele'', Tender Husband, v. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|That politician ''tops his part'' Who readily can lie with art. {{right|''Gay'', The Squire and his Cur.}}}} {{smaller|'''To top up''', to finish; wind up; put an end to: as, he was ''topped up'' by his extravagance. [Colloq.]}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To rise aloft; be eminent; tower; hence, to surpass; excel. See ''topping'', ''p. a.'' {{smaller block|But write thy best, and ''top''; and, in each line, Sir Formal's oratory will be thine. {{right|''Dryden'', MacFlecnoe, l. 167.}}}} '''2.''' To be of a (specified) height or top-measurement. {{smaller block|The latter was a dark chestnut with a white fetlock, standing full 16 hands (while the mare scarcely ''topped'' 15). {{right|''Lawrence'', Guy Livingstone, ix.}}}} '''3.''' To incline or fall with the top foremost; topple. {{smaller block|My attention was first called to a movement of the snow by noticing that the snow walls were leaving the building, as I at first supposed, by a ''topping'' movement. {{right|''Science'', X. 180.}}}} '''4'''†. To preen or prune one's self. {{smaller block|Always pruning, always cropping? Is her brightness still obscur'd? Ever dressing, ever ''topping?'' Always curing, never cur'd? {{right|''Quarles'', Emblems. (''Nares.'')}}}} '''To top over tail†''', to turn heels over head. See ''top over tail'', under ''top''1, ''n.'' {{smaller block|To tumble ouer and ouer, to ''toppe ouer tayle'', . . . may be also holesome for the body. {{right|''Ascham'', Toxophilus (ed. Arber), p. 47. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''To top up''' or '''off.''' (''a'') To finish; end up. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|Four engage to go half-price to the play at night, and ''top up'' with oysters. {{right|''Dickens'', Bleak House, xi.}}}} (''b'') See the quotation. {{smaller block|Strawberry pottles are often half cabbage leaves, a few tempting strawberries being displayed on the top of the pottle. "''Topping up'','' said a fruit dealer to me, "is the principal thing. . . . You ask any coster that knows the world, and he'll tell you that all the salesmen in the markets ''tops up''. It 's only making the best of it." {{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, I. 61.}}}} '''top1†''' (top), ''prep.'' [ME. ''toppe;'' short for ''on top of.''] Above. {{smaller block|This we bezechith ''toppe'' alle thing, thet thin holy name, thet is thi guode los, thi knaulechinge, thi beleaue, by y-confermed ine ous. ''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 106.}} '''top2''' (top), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''topped'', ppr. ''topping''. [Sc. also ''tope;'' < ME. ''toppen'', lit. 'catch by the top'; < ''top''1, ''n.'': see ''top''1.] '''I.†''' ''intrans.'' To wrestle; strive. {{smaller block|''Toppyn'', or fechte by the nekke [var. feyten, fyȝth, fythe, feightyn by the nek], colluctor. ''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 496.}} {{smaller block|As hi wexe hi ''toppede'' ofte ther nas bituene hem no love. {{right|''Poems and Lives of the Saints'' (ed. Furnivall), xxiv. 15.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' To oppose; resist. ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.] {{smaller block|The King nominated one day, in face of parliament, [the Earl of Mortoun]; while Argyle ''topes'' this nomination, as of a man unmeet.{{right|''Baillie'', Letters, I. 390.}}}} ¶ '''top'''2† (top), ''n.'' [< ''top''2, ''v.''] Opposition; struggle; conflict. {{smaller block|And the nations were angry: The world was in ''tops'' with Christ's church, having hatred against his people.{{right|''Durham'', Expos. of the Revelation, xi. 18.}}{{right|[(''Jamieson'', under ''tope.'')}}}} '''top'''3 (top), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''toppe''; < ME. ''top'', prob. < MD. ''top'', ''toppe'', var. (due to confusion with ''top'', point, summit) of ''dop'', ''doppe'', a top (cf. MD. ''dol'', var. of ''tol'', D. ''tol'', a top), = OHG. ''topf'', ''tof'', ''topfo'', MHG. ''topf'', ''toppe'', top, wheel, G. (dial.) ''topf'' = Dan. ''top'', a top, spinning-top; perhaps so called from a fancied resemblance to a pot, < MHG. ''topf'', ''tupfen'', G. ''topf'' (obs.), ''töpfen'', pot; cf. G. (dial.) ''dipfi'', ''dupfi'', ''dippen'', an iron kettle with three legs, prob. connected with AS. ''deóp'', G. ''tief'', etc., deep: see ''deep''. The notion that the top is so called "because it is sharpened to a tip or top on which it is spun," or "from whirling round on its top or point," is inconsistent with the G. forms (G. ''topf'', a top (toy), G. ''zopf'', a tuft, crest); moreover, a top does not spin on its top.] 1. A children's toy of conical, ovoid, or circular shape, whether solid or hollow, sometimes of wood with a point of metal, sometimes entirely of metal, made to whirl on its point by the rapid unwinding of a string wound about it, or by lashing with a whip, or by utilizing the power of a spring. All tops are more precisely called ''spinning-tops'', conical ones ''peg-tops'', and those that are lashed ''whip-tops''. {{smaller block|The chekker was choisly there chosen the first, The draghtes, the dyse, and other dregh gaumes, . . . The tables, the ''top'', tregetre also. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1624.}}}} {{smaller block|A ''toppe'' can I set, and dryve it in his kynde. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Pageant, Int. to Utopia, p. lxv.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''top'' was used in remote times by the Grecian boys. It is mentioned by Suidas, and . . . was well known at Rome in the days of Virgil, and with us as early at least as the fourteenth century. {{right|''Strutt'', Sports and Pastimes, p. 491.}}}} 2. In ''rope-making'', a conical block of wood with longitudinal grooves on its surface, in which the strands of the rope slide in the process of twisting.—'''Gyroscopic top.''' See ''gyroscopic.''—'''Parish top.''' See ''parish.''—'''Top and scourge''', a whip-top and its whip. ''Halliwell.'' [[File:century v08 p0188 c3f1.png|center|179px]] {{c|Top for Rope-making.}} '''toparch''' (tō′pärk), ''n.'' [= F. ''toparque'', < L. ''toparcha'', < Gr. τοπάρχης, the governor of a district, < τόπος, a place, + ἀρχειν, rule.] The governor of a district or toparchy. {{smaller block|The prince and ''toparch'' of that country. {{right|''Fuller.''}}}} '''toparchia''' (tō-pär′ki-ä), ''n.'' [L.: see ''toparchy.''] Same as ''toparchy.'' ''Athenæum'', No. 3267, p. 743.
